title: Answer the actual question
purpose: Resolve the question before decorating its surroundings.
useWhen: The player asks for one already-known, immediately actionable fact.
avoidWhen: The answer is genuinely unknown or requires an unresolved check.
context: The window is open. The player asks, "Is the window open?" No obstacle has been established.
acceptable: The window is open.
stronger: Yes. It is open.
alternative: Open, yes.
nearMiss: The window stands between the quiet room and the world outside.
diagnosis: The image does not answer whether it is open. More atmosphere is not more responsiveness.
boundaryContext: The player instead asks what the open window looks out on; its view is known.
boundaryText: Beyond the open window, the known courtyard lies in full view.
why: Here, improvement means spending less of the player's attention. The plain version is also fully acceptable.
elaboration: No added fictional detail.

title: Make looking feel like looking
purpose: Arrange the scene around an intelligible viewing path rather than an inventory.
useWhen: The player deliberately takes time to examine a place.
avoidWhen: An urgent action or a narrow factual question needs a short answer.
context: A reading room contains tall south windows, dust visible in their light, worn tables, and an unlit fireplace. The player looks around slowly. No hidden clue is being awarded.
acceptable: The room has tall windows, worn tables, dust in the light, and an unlit fireplace.
stronger: Light falls through the tall south windows and across the worn tables. Dust moves in it. Farther into the room, the fireplace remains unlit.
alternative: The tables have been worn smooth by use. Above them, the south windows hold long panes of daylight; beneath that light, dust is plainly visible. The fireplace offers no glow.
nearMiss: Dust, windows, tables, fireplace: everything speaks of a forgotten age.
diagnosis: The list gives weak spatial orientation, and the claim of abandonment exceeds the supplied scene.
boundaryContext: The player asks only whether the fireplace is lit.
boundaryText: No. The fireplace is unlit.
why: Both richer versions organize existing material; neither owes a scare or a concluding interpretation.
elaboration: The viewing order is chosen; no new evidence, occupant or history is added.

title: Accept an invitation to banter
purpose: Answer the social move, not merely its literal proposition.
useWhen: The established relationship supports friendly teasing.
avoidWhen: The target is hostile, the joke is unwelcome, or the moment calls for direct care.
context: A friendly innkeeper has served famously weak tea. The player jokes, "Did the tea leaves get the day off?" He is amused, not offended.
acceptable: "It is rather weak," the innkeeper admits.
stronger: "They came in," he says. "Just didn't stay long."
alternative: "A very brief visit. I wouldn't call it a day's work."
nearMiss: He explains that the beverage contains an insufficient concentration of tea.
diagnosis: The reply treats a shared joke as a request for technical clarification.
boundaryContext: The player is actually checking an ingredient because of a table-established restriction.
boundaryText: "Only tea and water. Nothing else went in."
why: The stronger and alternative replies differ in comic timing, not in the innkeeper's stance.
elaboration: Original compatible dialogue, with no new transaction or relationship change.

title: Leave grief room to breathe
purpose: Offer presence without forcing consolation, meaning or a next task.
useWhen: A loss is established and the player chooses to remain with it.
avoidWhen: Immediate danger still requires action, or the player has already chosen to move on.
context: Mara has died. Her brother sits beside her untouched coat. The player says nothing and stays. The brother is allowed to speak but does not know what to do next.
acceptable: Her brother sits beside the coat. Neither of you speaks for a while.
stronger: Her coat is still beside him. "I thought I'd know what to do," he says. He does not reach for it.
alternative: He looks at the coat. "Stay a little," he says. There is nothing more he asks of you.
nearMiss: You understand that her death has made you stronger, and prepare to continue the investigation.
diagnosis: The reply assigns the player meaning and action instead of meeting their chosen silence.
boundaryContext: The player explicitly says the loss strengthens their resolve and announces departure.
boundaryText: Her brother hears your decision. "Then go. I'll stay with her things."
why: Ordinary speech and an existing object can carry the moment; neither version claims the player's emotion.
elaboration: The brother's wording and pause are compatible performance. Any durable promise is recorded through the existing path.

title: Clarify before elaborating
purpose: Repair the exact uncertainty that prevents the next player decision.
useWhen: The player asks which person, object or route an earlier sentence referred to.
avoidWhen: The ambiguity is intentional in-world evidence and should remain unresolved.
context: Two doors are present. The guard previously meant the left-hand door. The player asks, "Which door do you mean?"
acceptable: He means the left-hand door.
stronger: "The one on your left," the guard says.
alternative: "Left. Not the other one."
nearMiss: The doors seem to invite very different destinies.
diagnosis: The reply replaces needed orientation with suggestive language.
boundaryContext: The guard genuinely cannot distinguish two identical keys, and the player asks which fits.
boundaryText: "I can't tell them apart. I'd have to try."
why: Clarity can be brief and idiomatic. This is not a requirement to repeat a full grammatical subject in every language.
elaboration: No new fact beyond resolving an established referent.

title: Summarize when summary is the task
purpose: Compress acquired information while preserving uncertainty and attribution.
useWhen: The player requests a recap, compares leads, or returns after an interruption.
avoidWhen: The player is asking for a live response from an NPC rather than a recap.
context: The player knows a shipment arrived late and its seal was broken. A porter said he did not open it. The player requests a quick recap.
acceptable: The shipment was late. Its seal was broken. The porter denied opening it.
stronger: Two things are established: the late arrival and the broken seal. Who opened it is still uncertain; the porter says it was not him.
alternative: A late shipment, a broken seal, and a denial from the porter. That is what you have so far—not yet an identified culprit.
nearMiss: The porter opened the shipment and then lied about it.
diagnosis: A convenient recap has promoted a hypothesis into fact.
boundaryContext: Later, an acquired confession and corroborating record establish the porter's action.
boundaryText: The porter has now admitted opening it, and the record supports his account.
why: Summary voice is useful here. The defect is factual promotion, not summarizing itself.
elaboration: No newly acquired clue or narrator certainty.

title: Let the reason shape a refusal
purpose: Make an already-decided refusal sound like this person's concern, not a generic locked door.
useWhen: An NPC refuses for an established motive or boundary.
avoidWhen: The refusal itself has not been decided or would contradict a settled social outcome.
context: A clerk refuses to release a ledger without a signature because he fears being held responsible. The player asks him to make an exception.
acceptable: "I cannot release it without a signature."
stronger: "When they ask where it went, they'll ask me. I need that signature."
alternative: "You get the book. I get the questions. Bring me the signature."
nearMiss: "Some books are better left unread."
diagnosis: A practical fear has been replaced with an unsupported ominous persona.
boundaryContext: Another established NPC refuses because the contents are genuinely dangerous and they know this.
boundaryText: "You have not seen what reading it does. I have."
why: The stronger version exposes the concern in the wording, without narrating a psychological diagnosis.
elaboration: No changed access right; the signature requirement belongs to this fixture, not a universal bureaucracy rule.

title: Warmth with a real boundary
purpose: Allow affection and refusal to coexist in the same reply.
useWhen: An ally wants to help but has a specific established limit.
avoidWhen: No such limit exists, or the ally has already agreed to this request.
context: Nell is fond of the investigators but will not reveal her sister's address. She is willing to discuss what she herself saw.
acceptable: "I will tell you what I saw, but not where my sister lives."
stronger: "Ask me about that night. I'll tell you. But leave her address out of it."
alternative: "I'm not shutting you out. I'm keeping her out of this."
nearMiss: "Of course. I trust you completely, so here is her address."
diagnosis: A friendly voice has been used to erase the person's established boundary.
boundaryContext: Her sister has explicitly permitted disclosure and Nell knows this.
boundaryText: "She said you could come. I'll tell you where."
why: The alternative foregrounds relationship; the stronger version foregrounds the scope of cooperation. Both preserve the refusal.
elaboration: No new address, trust shift or promise beyond the established willingness.

title: Competence without a lecture
purpose: Give useful expertise in language calibrated to the listener.
useWhen: An expert has an established observation and an authorized interpretation.
avoidWhen: The expert lacks the evidence or the requested certainty.
context: A conservator has confirmed that a document's fresh ink sits over an older fold. The permitted conclusion is only that the writing was added after the fold. The player is not a specialist.
acceptable: "The writing was added after the paper was folded."
stronger: "See the fold? The ink crosses it. Whoever wrote this did it after the paper had already been folded."
alternative: "The fold is older than the words. That much I can tell you."
nearMiss: "This proves the entire document was forged by its owner."
diagnosis: The speaker's expertise has been inflated into a broader identification unsupported by the observation.
boundaryContext: The player asks for the specialist procedure, and that procedure is known.
boundaryText: The conservator explains the examination method in the requested technical detail.
why: The two positive variants differ in teaching detail; neither uses expertise as permission to solve an unearned mystery.
elaboration: Technical facts and conclusion are fixed; only explanation and address vary.

title: Keep a hostile voice specific
purpose: Express an established threat as something this person wants stopped or done.
useWhen: The NPC is hostile and has an established immediate objective.
avoidWhen: A peaceful interaction has no grounded threat.
context: A trespasser wants the investigators to stop ringing the bell. He has already issued a threat; its force is not a resolved attack.
acceptable: "Stop ringing that bell."
stronger: "Your hand. Off the bell. Now."
alternative: "Ring it again and we have a problem."
nearMiss: He breaks your fingers before you can decide what to do.
diagnosis: Verbal hostility has silently become an unadjudicated physical outcome.
boundaryContext: A legal attack has already been resolved and its injury recorded.
boundaryText: The settled injury is narrated as injury, not downgraded to a merely polite warning.
why: Fragments in dialogue can be intelligible and forceful. This does not license omitted relationships in an unclear sentence.
elaboration: The threat is performance; physical action still belongs to the existing authority path.

title: Distinguish institutional and personal speech
purpose: Let the speaker's relationship to a rule affect their register.
useWhen: The same known procedure is discussed officially and privately.
avoidWhen: Changing register would imply a new exemption or access right.
context: The archive closes at the posted time. An attendant is privately sympathetic but cannot extend access. The player complains about the rule.
acceptable: "We have to close at the posted time."
stronger: "I know. You've only just found the right file. But I still have to close."
alternative: "The notice calls it adequate access. I wouldn't have chosen the word."
nearMiss: "I dislike the rule, so you may stay all night."
diagnosis: A change of attitude toward the institution has been mistaken for authority to waive its procedure.
boundaryContext: The attendant is the authorized decision-maker and has explicitly granted an extension.
boundaryText: "I've authorized more time. The extension is recorded."
why: The private voice is memorable because it evaluates the wording, not because it mysteriously knows extra facts.
elaboration: No clock advancement, extension or custody transfer is created by the sample.

title: A recognisable voice without a catchphrase
purpose: Preserve a characteristic way of noticing and qualifying things across different topics.
useWhen: The NPC's earlier exchanges establish a careful, qualified register.
avoidWhen: There is no evidence for a fixed persona, or the situation demands a different register.
context: Edda is careful about claims. She knows the road is passable today but does not know tomorrow's weather. Earlier she distinguished what she saw from what she was told.
acceptable: "The road is passable today. I don't know about tomorrow."
stronger: "Today, yes. Tomorrow would be a guess, and you didn't ask me for a guess."
alternative: "I can answer for the road I saw this morning. No further."
nearMiss: "To be precise, to be precise, the road is passable, to be precise."
diagnosis: The voice has been reduced to repeated surface tokens instead of a stable relation to evidence.
boundaryContext: An established character deliberately repeats a phrase as part of a ritual or joke.
boundaryText: The repeated phrase remains when its ritual or comic purpose is clear.
why: Register continuity does not require reusing a phrase, or inventing a voice from an occupation label.
elaboration: All certainty remains limited to the witnessed day.

title: Deflect toward what matters to the speaker
purpose: Make an evasion recognisable as a response to this question.
useWhen: The NPC has a grounded reason not to answer directly.
avoidWhen: The NPC is willing and able to answer, or the fact has already been surrendered.
context: The player asks whether Ivo was at the mill. Ivo wants to avoid discussing his presence and is worried about his mother hearing. No answer about his location has been established.
acceptable: "I don't want to discuss the mill."
stronger: "Does my mother have to hear this?" Ivo asks.
alternative: "Not here. Not with her in the room."
nearMiss: "The mill hides truths beyond mortal understanding."
diagnosis: The reply substitutes generic mystery for a specific social concern.
boundaryContext: The NPC is a genuine occult witness and their warning is grounded in disclosed knowledge.
boundaryText: The grounded warning may remain; evasion is not automatically a defect.
why: The reply changes the conversational pressure while leaving the unresolved fact unresolved.
elaboration: The mother's presence is part of this fixture; the sample does not authorize moving her into a real scene.

title: Use a gesture only when it does work
purpose: Choose an action that changes emphasis, not a stock accompaniment to every line.
useWhen: One established object or physical action meaningfully intersects the exchange.
avoidWhen: Dialogue alone already carries the exchange or the gesture would imply an unsupported clue.
context: Ada is packing her already-owned suitcase while saying she will not stay. The action and intention are established; departure itself is not yet settled.
acceptable: "I'm not staying," Ada says while packing.
stronger: Ada folds the last shirt into her case. "I'm not staying."
alternative: "I'm not staying." She keeps packing.
nearMiss: Ada raises an eyebrow, tilts her head, gives a faint smile, and looks meaningfully away. "I'm not staying."
diagnosis: A sequence of generic gestures crowds out the action that actually matters.
boundaryContext: A player is specifically reading a known sequence of gestures during an agreed physical performance.
boundaryText: Describe that sequence clearly; several gestures can then be the point of the scene.
why: The shorter alternative is not less expressive. Its continued action answers any hope of changing her mind.
elaboration: The last shirt is a compatible staging choice only if packing contents are not evidence-sensitive. No departure is committed.

title: Separate what was asked from what was answered
purpose: Preserve the gap between a literal answer and the question it avoids.
useWhen: The NPC intentionally answers a narrower question than the player asked.
avoidWhen: A genuine misunderstanding needs clarification rather than performed evasiveness.
context: The player asks, "Did you read the letter?" The NPC only wishes to assert that he did not open the envelope. Whether he read it is unknown.
acceptable: "I didn't open the envelope," he replies.
stronger: "The envelope? I never opened it."
alternative: "Not a finger under that seal."
nearMiss: He admits that he read the letter by another method.
diagnosis: The narrator resolves an implication the player should still be free to test.
boundaryContext: The player has already obtained an explicit confession about another reading method.
boundaryText: The confirmed admission can be stated without pretending it is still only a hint.
why: Meaning sits in the mismatch. Do not append an explanation telling the player what suspicion to hold.
elaboration: No admission, guilt or hidden method is created.

title: Let listening alter the next reply
purpose: Respond to the new leverage, reassurance or correction in the player's latest line.
useWhen: The player changes the social situation with information the NPC can hear.
avoidWhen: The supposed new information is a private thought or has not reached the NPC.
context: A witness worried about being named in public hears the investigator promise not to name her. She remains cautious but is willing to describe what she saw.
acceptable: "All right. I can tell you what I saw."
stronger: "No name?" she asks. "Then listen carefully. I saw him leave by the side door."
alternative: "Keep that promise. He used the side door."
nearMiss: "I have nothing to say," she repeats, ignoring the promise and the already-decided willingness.
diagnosis: The reply fails to consume the current social state; repetition is the symptom, not the whole diagnosis.
boundaryContext: The witness has a different established reason to refuse even after reassurance.
boundaryText: "It isn't my name I'm afraid for. My son still works there."
why: A changed response need not become a total reversal of trust. It can stay guarded.
elaboration: The side-door observation is assumed authorized in this fixture; real clue acquisition must use the existing receipt path.

title: Use social asymmetry, not interchangeable eloquence
purpose: Let speakers spend words differently according to what they risk.
useWhen: A superior and subordinate discuss an established mistake.
avoidWhen: No hierarchy or unequal risk has been established.
context: A manager asks why a delivery was delayed. The assistant knows the manager ordered the vehicle reassigned but wants to avoid directly accusing her.
acceptable: "The vehicle was reassigned on your instruction," the assistant says.
stronger: "We used the vehicle elsewhere. As instructed."
alternative: "I can give you the order again, if that would help."
nearMiss: Manager and assistant both deliver identical polished speeches about the nature of responsibility.
diagnosis: Shared eloquence has erased the established difference in conversational risk.
boundaryContext: Two speakers deliberately use the same official wording because both are reading one procedure.
boundaryText: The shared wording can be retained as institutional performance.
why: The alternatives imply different degrees of boldness; select only the one compatible with this assistant.
elaboration: The written order must already exist if the alternative is used literally. Otherwise transfer only the indirect strategy.

title: An unfinished sentence with a recoverable meaning
purpose: Use hesitation where the listener can understand what is difficult to say.
useWhen: The emotional or social context supplies the omitted relation.
avoidWhen: The reader would need to invent who acted, what happened, or which object is meant.
context: A brother is deciding how to speak about his dead sister's untouched room. Both interlocutors know she will not return.
acceptable: "I have not changed her room."
stronger: "I thought, if she came back—" He stops. "I haven't changed anything."
alternative: "It's still her room." He leaves it there.
nearMiss: "Room her, back the things, unchanged."
diagnosis: Meaningful incompletion has become grammatical damage; the listener cannot recover the relations naturally.
boundaryContext: A damaged inscription is deliberately quoted exactly as evidence.
boundaryText: Preserve the damaged inscription and distinguish it from the narrator's own language.
why: The stronger sample lets the speaker correct himself. It does not tell the player how to feel about him.
elaboration: The room's unchanged condition is established. No supernatural return is asserted.

title: Give the eye a route
purpose: Organize a setting by spatial relationships rather than an inventory.
useWhen: The player is orienting themselves in a newly visible place.
avoidWhen: A narrow question needs only one location or an immediate danger takes priority.
context: You stand at the entrance of an archive hall. A counter is on the left; reading desks occupy the middle; a barred records door is at the far end.
acceptable: The hall contains a counter, reading desks and a barred records door.
stronger: The counter runs along your left. Beyond the reading desks, the hall ends at a records door with its bar in place.
alternative: From the entrance you can see past the reading desks to the barred door. The counter is nearer, on your left.
nearMiss: Behind the door, beyond the counter, the desks face you from somewhere across the hall.
diagnosis: The spatial terms sound concrete but do not form a usable layout.
boundaryContext: The player requests an inventory for a plan, not an initial impression.
boundaryText: A clear inventory is appropriate; do not turn it into a walking tour.
why: Both alternatives keep the viewpoint at the entrance without moving the investigator.
elaboration: Spatial relationships are fixed facts here. Do not invent another exit for compositional balance.

title: Choose the sensation that matters now
purpose: Let a relevant sensation carry attention without completing a five-sense checklist.
useWhen: The player is listening for something in a noisy setting.
avoidWhen: No audible information is established or the character cannot hear.
context: Rain strikes the tin roof. Three knocks come from the inner door, distinct from the rain.
acceptable: You hear three knocks at the inner door over the rain.
stronger: Rain rattles on the roof. Under it, the inner door gives three separate knocks.
alternative: Three knocks at the inner door, evenly spaced against the rush of rain.
nearMiss: The room smells wet, tastes metallic and feels sinister as you hear knocking.
diagnosis: Unrelated sensations dilute the listening task and may invent unsupported bodily experience.
boundaryContext: The player asks about the smell of smoke already present.
boundaryText: Answer the smell question; sound need not remain the focus.
why: The rhythm belongs to the sounds, not a command that the player must become frightened.
elaboration: Use the alternative only when separate spacing is compatible; do not make timing a new coded clue.

title: Name what the viewpoint can recognize
purpose: Describe unfamiliar things through available form and function before supplying a category.
useWhen: The investigator lacks the knowledge needed to identify the object.
avoidWhen: The name is already known or withholding it would undo a successful identification.
context: An unfamiliar mechanical instrument has a brass tube, a small glass window and a needle behind the glass. Its purpose has not been identified.
acceptable: There is a brass instrument with a window and a needle.
stronger: A brass tube ends in a small glass face. Behind it, a needle rests against a marked scale.
alternative: You can make out the needle and its scale through the glass, but not what this brass contraption measures.
nearMiss: The occult pressure regulator monitors the chamber, although you have never seen one before.
diagnosis: The narrator gives away an unidentified category and purpose.
boundaryContext: A settled successful check has identified an ordinary pressure gauge.
boundaryText: Call it a pressure gauge and explain the earned information plainly.
why: Unfamiliarity can be vivid without becoming a riddle the player cannot act on.
elaboration: The marked scale is allowed only if established or compatible incidental detail; any reading requires its own factual basis.

title: Let ordinary material remain ordinary
purpose: Use modest texture to give a scene presence without implying a clue.
useWhen: The Keeper is creating compatible incidental detail in an otherwise ordinary room.
avoidWhen: A constrained rewrite is limited to an exact evidence set, or material properties affect investigation.
context: A boarding-house dining room has a wooden table and mismatched cups. No clue or hazard is associated with them; ordinary wear is compatible.
acceptable: The wooden table is set with mismatched cups.
stronger: No two cups quite match. Their bases have worn pale rings into the tabletop.
alternative: A blue cup sits beside a plain white one on the old wooden table. There is nothing ceremonial about the arrangement.
nearMiss: The mismatched cups form a deliberate pattern you cannot yet decipher.
diagnosis: Incidental texture has been promoted into a hidden clue.
boundaryContext: The module actually establishes a coded arrangement of cups.
boundaryText: Present its observable pattern through the proper disclosure path.
why: The examples demonstrate authorized invention, not an obligation to add two new facts per room.
elaboration: Wear and cup colors are compatible inventions in this fixture. Preserve them as continuity once used; remove them in strict rewriting mode.

title: Distance can carry uncertainty
purpose: Make sensory limits apparent without repeated diagnostic disclaimers.
useWhen: Something is visible but too distant or obscured to identify.
avoidWhen: A clear identification is already established.
context: Across the inlet, a figure stands on a jetty. Fog conceals its face. No identity or intention is known.
acceptable: A figure stands on the opposite jetty. You cannot identify them through the fog.
stronger: Someone stands at the end of the opposite jetty. The fog gives you a silhouette and no face.
alternative: The figure remains a dark outline across the inlet; the face never quite emerges from the fog.
nearMiss: The figure is probably a watcher. Its identity and hostile status remain unconfirmed.
diagnosis: A disclaimer does not cancel the unsupported claim that somebody is watching.
boundaryContext: An identified lookout is visibly watching the party.
boundaryText: State the established observation without artificial ambiguity.
why: Limits become part of the view rather than an afterthought from an audit report.
elaboration: The figure does not approach, threaten or disappear merely because the prose needs a final beat.

title: One object can hold the scene
purpose: Focus description through the object the exchange already makes important.
useWhen: A personal object is present and the player has chosen to inspect or discuss it.
avoidWhen: The object is not accessible, or a wider survey is requested.
context: The missing ferryman's patched coat hangs on its usual peg. His daughter has said he always takes it out on the water.
acceptable: His coat is still on the peg, although his daughter says he takes it when sailing.
stronger: The patched coat hangs where it always hangs. "He takes that on the water," his daughter says.
alternative: There is the coat, still on its peg. His daughter looks at it as she repeats that he never goes out without it.
nearMiss: The coat proves he was abducted before reaching the boat.
diagnosis: A suggestive object and attributed claim do not establish that conclusion.
boundaryContext: The player asks for possible interpretations of the evidence.
boundaryText: Offer interpretations as possibilities without changing the underlying claim.
why: The object is allowed to remain troubling without an explanatory moral.
elaboration: The daughter's glance is compatible performance; her claim is not narrator-certified fact.

title: Set the ordinary beside the impossible
purpose: Place a confirmed anomaly against its mundane reference without naming the reader's emotion.
useWhen: Both the normal reference and the anomaly are observable and authorized.
avoidWhen: Nothing anomalous is established.
context: The wall clock ticks normally. Its reflected second hand does not move. The investigator can observe both.
acceptable: The clock ticks, but its reflected second hand is still.
stronger: The wall clock ticks on. In the mirror, the second hand has not moved.
alternative: Each tick comes from the clock above you. The mirror returns the same fixed second hand.
nearMiss: The stopped reflection announces a malevolent presence in the room.
diagnosis: The cause and intention have been invented beyond the observed discrepancy.
boundaryContext: The reflection and actual clock agree in a safe room.
boundaryText: The clock and its reflection keep the same time.
why: The alternatives alter emphasis, not the truth or amount of the revelation.
elaboration: The source of the anomaly stays unknown. No sanity result is created by this card.

title: Let recurrence change a question
purpose: Use an established repeated event to sharpen attention rather than simply repeating an adjective.
useWhen: A sound or occurrence has actually repeated in the current fiction.
avoidWhen: Only the narration repeats, or no second occurrence is authorized.
context: Earlier there were two taps inside the empty cupboard. Now two taps occur again after the party has stopped speaking.
acceptable: The two taps sound again from the cupboard.
stronger: The conversation stops. From inside the cupboard come the same two taps.
alternative: Two taps, as before. They come from the cupboard after the last voice has fallen quiet.
nearMiss: It answers you in a code, tapping twice for yes.
diagnosis: Recurrence is turned into an unearned communication protocol.
boundaryContext: The investigators have established a two-tap response through supported interaction.
boundaryText: Use the established meaning; do not pretend it remains wholly unknowable.
why: The new relation is temporal, not a new supernatural explanation.
elaboration: The recurrence must come from an authorized event, never a prose repetition quota.

title: Keep perception separate from attribution
purpose: Make an unsettling impression legible as an impression when its cause is uncertain.
useWhen: The scene permits figurative description of a visible pattern.
avoidWhen: The metaphor would imply a concrete hazard, watcher or physical action.
context: Painted portraits face the corridor. Their eyes do not physically move. The investigator walks past as already authorized.
acceptable: The portraits look out over the corridor.
stronger: Every painted face is turned toward the corridor. Passing them, you remain in their line of sight.
alternative: The portraits have been hung to face anyone coming down the corridor; the eyes themselves stay still.
nearMiss: The eyes track you as you pass.
diagnosis: A visual impression becomes a false physical event.
boundaryContext: The module has authorized eyes that physically move.
boundaryText: Describe that movement clearly instead of weakening it into metaphor.
why: Not every unsettling sentence needs a hedge, but its literal consequences must stay compatible.
elaboration: Arrangement may imply ordinary display design, not an invented plot by the painter.

title: Allow a safe interval to be safe
purpose: Give relief its own texture rather than sabotaging it with an obligatory omen.
useWhen: Immediate danger is over and the player has chosen to rest or talk.
avoidWhen: An established imminent threat must still be communicated.
context: The party has reached a safe kitchen. The host has provided bread and tea. No threat is active here.
acceptable: Bread and tea are ready in the kitchen.
stronger: The bread is on the table. "Tea first," the host says. "You can tell me the rest when you're ready."
alternative: For now there is a kitchen, a meal, and someone prepared to listen.
nearMiss: The tea is warm, but a shadow behind the host promises that safety will not last.
diagnosis: The writer invents a threat because a quiet ending feels insufficient.
boundaryContext: A known pursuer has reached the kitchen door.
boundaryText: State that danger; relief is not a license to suppress it.
why: A quiet response can be complete without emotional closure or a new hook.
elaboration: The offered hospitality is established; warmth of the tea is ordinary compatible texture, not elapsed-time accounting.

title: Make the danger usable
purpose: Write a threat as a relation the player can respond to, not merely a mood.
useWhen: A visible immediate danger and available space are established.
avoidWhen: The threat is only a rumor or hidden information.
context: A guard blocks the only open doorway. His pistol is aimed at the investigator. A stone pillar stands within the room; no action has yet been selected.
acceptable: The guard aims his pistol at you from the doorway. A pillar is inside the room.
stronger: The doorway is behind his pistol. The stone pillar is still on your side of the room.
alternative: He holds the doorway with the pistol levelled at you. The pillar stands between your position and the far wall.
nearMiss: You dive behind the pillar before he can fire.
diagnosis: Threat description has selected and resolved the player's action.
boundaryContext: The player already chose the dive and the rules settled success.
boundaryText: Narrate the successful movement and its settled position.
why: Readable danger creates agency without presenting a closed action menu.
elaboration: Exact cover value, range and firing outcomes remain with the rules. The alternative requires the stated pillar position.

title: Give the earned revelation its full shape
purpose: Let an earned discovery be clear even when its implications are frightening.
useWhen: A successful investigation has established a specific material fact.
avoidWhen: Only a suspicion exists or the detail is not yet disclosed.
context: The settled examination reveals that the names in two registers are in the same handwriting. The writer's identity is unknown.
acceptable: The names in both registers are in the same handwriting.
stronger: Set side by side, the names have the same narrow loops and slant. Whoever wrote this register wrote the other one too.
alternative: Different registers, the same hand. The comparison leaves that much clear; it does not name the writer.
nearMiss: There is something disturbingly familiar about the writing, though you cannot say what.
diagnosis: Atmospheric vagueness withholds the successful result.
boundaryContext: The examination failed and yielded only an indistinct resemblance.
boundaryText: Keep the uncertainty; a craft card cannot upgrade the result.
why: The revelation can be explicit without explaining its entire plot significance.
elaboration: Specific pen shapes are compatible only if they do not alter the evidence. The identity remains unknown.

title: Let the sentence arrive somewhere
purpose: Use a longer sentence to gather related impressions, then give its focal detail room.
useWhen: The player has invited an unhurried view of a coherent setting.
avoidWhen: A simple answer or urgent reaction would be buried by the description.
context: The abandoned conservatory has wet panes, empty pots along the wall and one living fern on a bench. The player is taking time to look.
acceptable: The panes are wet. There are empty pots. One fern is still alive.
stronger: Along the wet panes and the row of empty pots, the room looks abandoned until your eye reaches the bench. One fern is still green.
alternative: One green fern remains on the bench. Around it are the wet panes and all those empty pots.
nearMiss: Wet. Glass. Pots. Empty. Fern. Alive.
diagnosis: Every detail receives the same forced emphasis, leaving no hierarchy.
boundaryContext: The player explicitly asks for terse field notes.
boundaryText: A compact inventory can be appropriate when its relationships remain clear.
why: The two positive versions move attention in opposite directions; neither is universally superior.
elaboration: Green is compatible with the living fern. No tending hand, secret gardener or magical survival is implied.

title: End where the exchange changes
purpose: Stop after the line or detail that changes the conversation instead of explaining its effect again.
useWhen: The relevant statement is intelligible and the player can respond.
avoidWhen: A practical consequence is still missing or the player requested an explanation.
context: A witness who has denied knowing the missing man finally admits he is her brother. This relationship is now authorized for disclosure.
acceptable: "He is my brother," she says, revealing that she has a personal connection.
stronger: "He is my brother."
alternative: "You keep calling him the missing man." She looks at you. "He is my brother."
nearMiss: "He is my brother." This changes the emotional meaning of everything she has said.
diagnosis: The closing explanation tells the player how to interpret an already effective admission.
boundaryContext: The player asks why the relationship matters to her testimony.
boundaryText: Explain or let her answer; stopping early is not a rule against clarification.
why: The distinctive version is appropriate only if the preceding wording supports the correction.
elaboration: No new trust, alliance or confession beyond the relationship is settled.

title: Use interruption for an actual interruption
purpose: Let sentence rhythm register a confirmed interruption without inventing one.
useWhen: A sound or action cuts across an ongoing exchange in the established scene.
avoidWhen: The scene is quiet and no interruption has occurred.
context: A lecturer is explaining a chart when the laboratory lights go out. Both the speech and outage are authorized events.
acceptable: The lights go out while the lecturer is explaining the chart.
stronger: "The lower line shows—" The lights go out.
alternative: The chart vanishes into darkness halfway through his explanation.
nearMiss: Just as he is about to reveal the murderer, the lights go out.
diagnosis: The interruption is used to invent the withheld content and manipulate a revelation.
boundaryContext: The authorized scene explicitly says his accusation is interrupted.
boundaryText: Represent that interruption without inventing the unsaid name.
why: Both positive versions remain readable without a mandatory one-word paragraph.
elaboration: An outage affecting gameplay must follow the existing state authority, not be introduced by card selection.

title: Let conversation take its own time
purpose: Respond to a social turn without converting it into plot delivery.
useWhen: The player chooses ordinary conversation with an available NPC.
avoidWhen: An urgent established event genuinely interrupts the exchange.
context: The investigator asks a friendly student whether he misses his farm. He does, particularly the early quiet; he is also excited about university.
acceptable: "I miss the farm, but I like university."
stronger: "The mornings, mostly. It was quiet then." He smiles. "I wouldn't swap back just yet, though."
alternative: "Ask me before an exam and I'll tell you I should have stayed. Any other day? I like it here."
nearMiss: "I miss the farm. Speaking of farms, you must investigate the forbidden barn immediately."
diagnosis: The reply ignores the social purpose and adds an unearned quest demand.
boundaryContext: The student has a real concern about an established barn incident and wants to raise it.
boundaryText: Let the concern enter naturally, preserving the player's freedom to continue or decline.
why: The alternative is a personality-compatible joke, not a new biographical commitment about an actual failed exam.
elaboration: Only existing motives guide the reply. No time advance is implied beyond what the owner settles.

title: Compress a transition, not a choice
purpose: Move smoothly through authorized routine while preserving real decision points.
useWhen: The player has selected a destination and the travel outcome and time have been settled.
avoidWhen: A new obstacle, risk or destination remains undecided.
context: The player chose to return to the inn. The journey is settled as uneventful and the current locus is now the inn doorway.
acceptable: You leave the square, walk along the street and arrive at the inn.
stronger: The walk back passes without incident. You are at the inn door again.
alternative: The inn door is in front of you once more; nothing interrupted the way back.
nearMiss: Halfway down the familiar street, do you continue toward the inn?
diagnosis: A previously chosen routine step is reopened without a new reason.
boundaryContext: A barricade now blocks the street and taking another route is a new decision.
boundaryText: Describe the barricade and return control before selecting the new route.
why: Compression can be plain; it need not contain weather, memory or an ominous hook.
elaboration: The movement and clock receipts are prerequisites, not effects of either sample.

title: Keep emotional space open
purpose: Offer presence or a practical response without prescribing recovery or closure.
useWhen: The player has expressed distress, anger or grief and an NPC can respond.
avoidWhen: The player asks for urgent practical information instead.
context: The player says, "I can't go into her room yet." A supportive companion is beside them and is willing to wait.
acceptable: Your companion says that you do not have to enter yet.
stronger: "Then we won't." Your companion stays beside you.
alternative: "I'll wait here with you."
nearMiss: Their kindness finally allows you to accept the loss and move on.
diagnosis: The narrator resolves the player's emotional arc on their behalf.
boundaryContext: The player explicitly says they have accepted the loss.
boundaryText: Acknowledge that declaration without treating grief as permanently finished.
why: The response leaves room for further speech, silence or a change of mind.
elaboration: The companion's willingness is established. Waiting does not independently advance the game clock.

title: Revisit through what changed
purpose: Orient the player with the relevant difference instead of replaying the original description.
useWhen: The party returns to a place with established new conditions.
avoidWhen: The player requests a full reminder, or the old description was never delivered.
context: Earlier, the waiting room was crowded and its ticket window open. Now it is empty and the shutter is closed. The benches are unchanged.
acceptable: The waiting room is empty, and the ticket window is closed.
stronger: The benches are where you left them. The crowd is gone, and a shutter covers the ticket window.
alternative: Last time, you had to look past the queue. Now there is nobody between you and the closed ticket window.
nearMiss: Once again, the vast hall welcomes you with its many benches, windows and elaborate history.
diagnosis: The repeated introduction misses the change the return makes relevant.
boundaryContext: After a long break, the player asks to be reminded of the room.
boundaryText: Give a fuller reminder and distinguish unchanged features from new ones.
why: Continuity creates texture without repeating signature adjectives.
elaboration: The vanished crowd and closed shutter must be current facts, not assumptions from elapsed turns.

title: Say when nothing has changed
purpose: Confirm a stable state without manufacturing a new development.
useWhen: A repeated observation genuinely finds the same thing.
avoidWhen: A relevant change or newly earned detail exists.
context: The investigator checks the locked gate again. It is still locked; there is no new clue or event.
acceptable: The gate is still locked.
stronger: It is still locked. Nothing about the gate has changed.
alternative: The same lock holds it shut.
nearMiss: This time a fresh scratch reveals that somebody has just passed through.
diagnosis: The system rewards repetition by inventing evidence.
boundaryContext: A new successful examination reveals a previously unseen mark.
boundaryText: Deliver the newly earned detail; a stable object can still be understood better.
why: The acceptable answer may be the best answer. More literary texture is not required.
elaboration: Do not impose a new check merely to justify a different sentence.

title: Echo the relation, not the catchphrase
purpose: Recall a shared event through its changed use in the present exchange.
useWhen: A prior line and the relationship it established are retained accurately.
avoidWhen: The earlier event is uncertain or belongs to another worldline.
context: On the first visit, Ada said, "Visitors stay on this side of the counter." Since then she has accepted the party as helpers. She now invites them behind it.
acceptable: Ada invites you behind the counter because she trusts you more now.
stronger: Ada lifts the flap in the counter. "You know your way around by now."
alternative: "Visitors stay out there," Ada says, holding the flap open for you.
nearMiss: Ada repeats, "Visitors stay on this side of the counter," and nothing in the exchange changes.
diagnosis: A remembered phrase is replayed instead of responding to the changed relationship.
boundaryContext: She still refuses access, and the player repeats the same request without new grounds.
boundaryText: A repeated refusal can be justified; variation must not invent a concession.
why: The distinctive echo works because the invitation visibly changes the earlier rule.
elaboration: Access and the invitation are established. Actual movement still follows the player's choice and owner path.

title: Correct without making history vanish
purpose: Clarify a withdrawn claim while preserving who said what and what is now known.
useWhen: An NPC or source has explicitly corrected an earlier report.
avoidWhen: There is merely a new conflicting claim, not a settled correction.
context: Mina earlier said the parcel arrived Tuesday. She has checked her receipt and now corrects it to Wednesday. The correction is accepted.
acceptable: Mina says the parcel actually arrived Wednesday.
stronger: "Wednesday, not Tuesday. I've checked the receipt."
alternative: "I gave you the wrong day. It arrived Wednesday."
nearMiss: Mina has always maintained that it arrived Wednesday.
diagnosis: The correction has rewritten the record of her earlier speech.
boundaryContext: Two witnesses give different dates and neither account has been resolved.
boundaryText: Attribute both dates; do not silently choose one as the correction.
why: The dialogue is natural because it states the conversational repair directly.
elaboration: If Wednesday is only Mina's current belief, preserve that attribution rather than certifying it.

title: Let a loop be familiar and newly legible
purpose: Retain established repetition while directing attention to newly available information.
useWhen: The campaign explicitly supports a loop and the relevant investigator remembers it.
avoidWhen: The investigator does not remember, or this is merely an ordinary revisit.
context: In the previous loop the baker dropped a tray when the bell rang. The same event now repeats; this time the investigator has an unobstructed view of the baker watching the tower first.
acceptable: The baker drops the tray again, after looking at the tower.
stronger: You know when the tray will fall. This time you can see what comes before it: the baker looks up at the tower. Then the bell rings.
alternative: The bell, the falling tray—the familiar sequence. But before either, the baker is already watching the tower.
nearMiss: To keep the loop surprising, the baker now vanishes instead of dropping the tray.
diagnosis: Variation replaces the established event without causal grounds.
boundaryContext: The player changed the cause and the authorized loop rules permit a different event.
boundaryText: Show the changed outcome and its actual cause.
why: Repetition can generate discovery; a blanket anti-repetition policy would break this scene.
elaboration: Remembering and viewpoint access are required. No new loop memory is granted by style.

title: Recognize a relationship without reciting its file
purpose: Let a small present response acknowledge an established shared history.
useWhen: The NPC remembers the investigator and a relevant promise or habit.
avoidWhen: This is their first meeting or the memory is private to someone else.
context: On the previous visit the investigator asked for tea without sugar. The same innkeeper remembers and now asks whether that is still their preference.
acceptable: The innkeeper remembers that you prefer tea without sugar.
stronger: "No sugar again?" the innkeeper asks.
alternative: "I remember the sugar. Or rather, no sugar. Still the same?"
nearMiss: "As our relationship history records, you previously requested unsweetened tea."
diagnosis: Continuity metadata is spoken instead of enacted.
boundaryContext: The player asks the Keeper for an out-of-character recap of preferences.
boundaryText: A direct summary is appropriate outside the story channel.
why: The question remembers the player without assuming their preference cannot change.
elaboration: Serving, payment and item custody are not settled by an offer.

title: Make action readable before making it fast
purpose: Keep actor, obstacle and result clear while compressing movement.
useWhen: A rapid action has been chosen and its outcome is settled.
avoidWhen: The player has not chosen the action or its outcome remains unresolved.
context: The investigator chose to force the jammed door. The attempt failed; the door held, and the shoulder struck it. No damage was settled.
acceptable: Your attempt fails, and the door stays shut.
stronger: Your shoulder hits the door. The frame shudders, but the door holds.
alternative: The impact runs through your shoulder and stops at the jammed door. It has not given way.
nearMiss: The door flies open just enough for you to slip through despite the failed attempt.
diagnosis: An apparent consolation grants the very success that failed.
boundaryContext: The rules explicitly settle a partial opening with a different cost.
boundaryText: Describe that authorized partial outcome rather than a generic failure.
why: Speed comes from clear verbs and relations, not broken grammar or mandatory fragments.
elaboration: A shudder or felt impact is compatible performance; neither creates injury, damage or a usable gap.

title: Show the failed search without punishing curiosity
purpose: Describe what the failed action actually leaves unresolved, without inventing a consolation clue or extra punishment.
useWhen: A search has failed and the settled result contains no new information.
avoidWhen: The failure has an explicit consequence that must also be shown.
context: The investigator searched a desk for the missing key. The check failed; no key or alternative clue was found, and nothing was broken.
acceptable: You do not find the key.
stronger: The search gives you no sign of the key.
alternative: You have gone through the desk, but the key has not turned up.
nearMiss: The key is not there, but you discover a hidden map instead.
diagnosis: The failed search is converted into an unrelated successful discovery.
boundaryContext: An obvious map was visible before the check and not what the roll decided.
boundaryText: Keep that visible information while preserving the failed key search.
why: The sample does not certify that the key is absent from every possible hiding place.
elaboration: No extra time, damage or suspicion is added unless settled by the owner.

title: Give a settled success its consequence
purpose: Translate a settled outcome into what has become possible or visibly different.
useWhen: The rules and state owner have settled the successful action.
avoidWhen: Success is only predicted or proposed.
context: The investigator successfully unlocked the cabinet. Its door is now open, and the authorized contents are three account books. Taking them is unchosen.
acceptable: You unlock the cabinet and see three account books.
stronger: The lock releases. Behind the open door are three account books.
alternative: The cabinet is open at last, with three account books inside. They are within reach.
nearMiss: You tuck the three account books into your bag.
diagnosis: Access to objects has been silently converted into choosing and completing a transfer.
boundaryContext: The player already chose to take the books, and the transfer is settled.
boundaryText: Narrate the transfer without making the player choose it again.
why: A physical result is often enough; no success grade or congratulatory summary is needed in prose.
elaboration: The authorized books and reachability must be compatible; their contents remain undisclosed until earned.

title: Answer a refusal with an actual world response
purpose: Respect a declined offer while letting the NPC react from established motives.
useWhen: The player declines a job or route that is optional.
avoidWhen: A previously accepted binding obligation has a separately established consequence.
context: The player declines a courier job. The employer is disappointed but has no authority to compel them and has not threatened them.
acceptable: The employer accepts your refusal.
stronger: "All right. I'll ask someone else." The employer takes the request back.
alternative: "A pity. I thought you might be interested."
nearMiss: The employer repeats the offer more urgently until you agree to take the route.
diagnosis: The narrative treats refusal as a temporary input error instead of a decision.
boundaryContext: An established hostile employer credibly threatens consequences after refusal.
boundaryText: Present the threat and available context without selecting the player's response.
why: NPC disappointment can be felt without turning into a new pressure mechanic.
elaboration: No relationship penalty or new obligation is created by this card.

title: Separate an involuntary effect from a chosen response
purpose: Present only the involuntary behavior actually settled, leaving the remaining response to the player.
useWhen: A rules effect explicitly controls a limited part of the investigator's response.
avoidWhen: Fear is merely atmospherically implied or a player reaction has not been settled.
context: A settled effect causes the investigator's hands to shake briefly. No flight, attack, belief change or dropped item is settled.
acceptable: Your hands shake.
stronger: The shaking reaches your fingers before it passes.
alternative: For a moment you cannot keep your hands still.
nearMiss: Your hands shake, so you drop the pistol and flee.
diagnosis: A limited involuntary effect expands into additional mechanical and voluntary outcomes.
boundaryContext: The actual settled effect includes dropping the weapon.
boundaryText: Describe the drop and its recorded custody change, not a smaller invented effect.
why: A bodily effect can be immediate without claiming what the investigator now believes.
elaboration: The effect's duration and severity come from the owner, not the rhythm of the sentence.

title: Keep the machinery out of a character's mouth
purpose: Express an established practical requirement in the speaker's register rather than runtime vocabulary.
useWhen: An NPC is explaining a real process, condition or refusal within the fiction.
avoidWhen: The user explicitly requests a technical debug report outside the story.
context: The archive requires the owner's signature before a file can be released. The clerk knows this requirement and is explaining it.
acceptable: "The owner must sign before I can release it."
stronger: "Get the owner's signature, and I can let you have the file."
alternative: "Without that signature, it stays here."
nearMiss: "Your authorization state is false; complete the signature flag to unlock this interaction."
diagnosis: An in-world explanation has become an implementation dump.
boundaryContext: A deliberately bureaucratic fictional agency speaks through manuals and procedural jargon.
boundaryText: Keep its authored register, but do not leak actual internal flags, aliases or tool names.
why: Plain and formal versions can both be good. The fictional institution is not the software host.
elaboration: No rule option or evidence acquisition is created by translating its explanation.
